claim: Male C57BL/6J mice (10-12 weeks of age) were intravasally injected with UPEC or saline vehicle alone (sham) after ligation of the vas deferens.
source: (A) Male C57BL/6J mice (10–12 weeks of age) were intravasally injected with UPEC or saline vehicle alone (sham) after ligation of the vas deferens.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental procedure shown in Figure 1A and described in the text.

claim: Bacteria were found in all epididymal regions (IS, caput, corpus, cauda) and in the testis 1 day post infection.
source: Bacteria were found in all epididymal regions (IS, caput, corpus, cauda) and in the testis 1 day p.i. (Figure 1B)
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B measuring bacterial loads.

claim: Bacteria persisted at high numbers only for up to 10 days in the cauda.
source: Bacteria were found in all epididymal regions (IS, caput, corpus, cauda) and in the testis 1 day p.i. (Figure 1B), but persisted at high numbers only for up to 10 days in the cauda (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by bacterial load measurements shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Bacteria are cleared toward day 30 post infection.
source: Later time points were not examined, as it is known that bacteria are cleared toward day 30 p.i. (Klein et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Klein et al., 2019.

claim: The caput showed no gross morphological alterations following UPEC infection.
source: In line with previous reports (Klein et al., 2020), the caput showed no gross morphological alterations (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–D)
evidence: This is supported by histological data in Figure 1C and supplemental figures, and corroborated by citation to Klein et al., 2020.

claim: Slight histopathological changes including mild focal epithelial damage and minor connective tissue deposition within the interstitium were observed in the caput 5 days post infection.
source: although slight histopathological changes, including mild focal epithelial damage and minor connective tissue deposition within the interstitium, were observed 5 days p.i. (Figure 1C)
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The caput disease score returned to normal values at 10 days post infection.
source: although slight histopathological changes, including mild focal epithelial damage and minor connective tissue deposition within the interstitium, were observed 5 days p.i. (Figure 1C) resulting in an elevated disease score that returned to normal values at 10 days p.i. (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by disease score data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Severe tissue remodeling was seen in the cauda following UPEC infection.
source: In accordance with previous studies from our group (Klein et al., 2020) severe tissue remodeling was seen in the cauda (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2)
evidence: This is supported by histological data in Figure 1E and supplemental figures, and corroborated by citation to Klein et al., 2020.

claim: Severe tissue remodeling in the cauda was characterized by infiltration of immune cells, loss of epithelial integrity, connective tissue deposition in the interstitium, reduction of luminal diameter, and epididymal duct destruction.
source: severe tissue remodeling was seen in the cauda (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 2) characterized by infiltration of immune cells, loss of epithelial integrity, connective tissue deposition in the interstitium, reduction of luminal diameter, and ultimately, epididymal duct destruction
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 1E and supplemental figures.

claim: Severe tissue remodeling in the cauda resulted in a significantly increased and persistent overall disease score.
source: characterized by infiltration of immune cells, loss of epithelial integrity, connective tissue deposition in the interstitium, reduction of luminal diameter, and ultimately, epididymal duct destruction resulting in a significantly increased and persistent overall disease score (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by disease score data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Immune cell infiltrates in the cauda were initially located peripherally at 5 days post infection before larger leukocytic conglomerates/granulomas developed within the entire cauda region.
source: Initially, immune cell infiltrates were predominantly located peripherally within the cauda (5 days p.i.) before larger leukocytic conglomerates/granulomas developed within the entire cauda region (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological observations shown in Figure 1 supplement 2.

claim: Sham control mice initially showed histopathological alterations in the cauda that were milder than in infected animals.
source: Sham control mice initially showed histopathological alterations in the cauda that were milder than in infected animals and returned to a level comparable to untreated epididymis toward day 10 p.i. (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1E, 1F, and supplemental figures.

claim: Sham control mice histopathological alterations in the cauda returned to a level comparable to untreated epididymis toward day 10 post infection.
source: Sham control mice initially showed histopathological alterations in the cauda that were milder than in infected animals and returned to a level comparable to untreated epididymis toward day 10 p.i. (Figure 1E and F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1E, 1F, and supplemental figures.

claim: Almost no transcriptional differences were identified between the caput of sham- and UPEC-infected mice (in total 5 differentially expressed genes).
source: In line with the minimal histopathological alterations, almost no transcriptional differences were identified between the caput of sham- and UPEC-infected mice (in total 5 differentially expressed genes (DEG), cut-off: FDR ≤0.05, –1 < logFC > 1, Figure 1G, Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1G and supplemental figures.

claim: The cauda of sham- and UPEC-infected mice showed considerable transcriptional differences (in total 5082 differentially expressed genes).
source: In contrast, the cauda of sham- and UPEC-infected mice showed considerable transcriptional differences (in total 5082 DEG, cut-off: FDS ≤0.05, –1 < logFC > 1, Figure 1g, Figure 1—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1G and supplemental figures.

claim: The transcriptional changes in the corpus were intermediate compared with those in caput and cauda epididymides.
source: As shown by principal component analysis (PCA), the transcriptional changes in the corpus were intermediate compared with those in caput and cauda epididymides (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is supported by PCA analysis shown in Figure 1 supplement 3A.

claim: The caput was highly enriched in transcripts encoding immunomodulatory factors, such as β-defensins, bactericidal permeability-increasing protein, and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1.
source: Compared to the cauda, the caput was highly enriched in transcripts encoding immunomodulatory factors, such as β-defensins, bactericidal permeability-increasing protein, and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1, with no changes in the high levels observed in sham- and UPEC-infected mice (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: There were no changes in the high levels of immunomodulatory factor transcripts in the caput between sham- and UPEC-infected mice.
source: Compared to the cauda, the caput was highly enriched in transcripts encoding immunomodulatory factors, such as β-defensins, bactericidal permeability-increasing protein, and indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase 1, with no changes in the high levels observed in sham- and UPEC-infected mice (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The cauda of UPEC-infected mice was characterized by an upregulation of numerous transcripts encoding pro-inflammatory mediators, including pro-inflammatory cytokines and chemoattractants.
source: In contrast, compared to sham control mice, the cauda of UPEC-infected mice was characterized by an upregulation of numerous transcripts encoding pro-inflammatory mediators, including pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g. Il-1α, Il-6, Il-17) and chemoattractants (e.g. Ccl2, Ccl3, Ccl4, Cxcl2, Cxcl5) as well as inflammasome-associated transcripts (e.g. Nlrp3, Il1b) (Figure 1H, Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: This is supported by RNAseq data shown in Figure 1H and supplemental figures.

claim: The cauda of UPEC-infected mice displayed upregulation of gene sets associated with fibrotic tissue remodeling and pro-inflammatory immune responses.
source: By grouping transcripts according to their gene ontology and pathway contribution, the cauda of UPEC-infected mice 10 days p.i. displayed upregulation of gene sets associated with fibrotic tissue remodeling and pro-inflammatory immune responses (e.g. positive regulation of NF kappa B – transcription factor activity, collagen fibril organization, and positive regulation of the ERK1 and ERK2 cascade, Figure 1I).
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Pathway analyses revealed an upregulation of gene sets associated with B and T cell activation in the cauda at 10 days post infection.
source: Further pathway analyses revealed an upregulation of gene sets associated with B and T cell activation, indicating a transition from the innate to the adaptive immune response at this stage of infection within the cauda (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by pathway analysis shown in Figure 1 supplement 3.

claim: The upregulation of gene sets associated with B and T cell activation indicates a transition from the innate to the adaptive immune response at 10 days post infection within the cauda.
source: Further pathway analyses revealed an upregulation of gene sets associated with B and T cell activation, indicating a transition from the innate to the adaptive immune response at this stage of infection within the cauda (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the pathway analysis data shown in Figure 1 supplement 3.

claim: The caput epididymidis of sham and infected mice were enriched with gene sets related to sperm maturation.
source: The caput epididymidis of sham and infected mice were enriched with gene sets related to sperm maturation (e.g. protein localization in cilium, cellular component assembly involved in morphogenesis, and regulation of cilia beating frequency, Figure 1I)
evidence: This is supported by gene set enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1I.

claim: Gene sets related to sperm maturation in the caput are indicative of normal epididymal function.
source: The caput epididymidis of sham and infected mice were enriched with gene sets related to sperm maturation (e.g. protein localization in cilium, cellular component assembly involved in morphogenesis, and regulation of cilia beating frequency, Figure 1I), indicative of normal epididymal function.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene set enrichment data.

claim: Disease progression correlated positively with the appearance and degree of immune cell infiltration in the cauda.
source: In line with the observed histopathological alterations and the transcriptional profile of the cauda of UPEC-infected mice, disease progression correlated positively with the appearance and degree of immune cell infiltration in this region (Figure 2A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2A and supplemental figures.

claim: An increase in the total immune cell population (CD45+) was observed in both the caput and cauda of sham mice with most immune cell infiltrates observed at day 5.
source: Notably, we observed an increase in the total immune cell population (CD45+) in both the caput and cauda of sham mice with most immune cell infiltrates observed at day 5, which returned to normal levels by day 14 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The immune cell population in sham mice returned to normal levels by day 14.
source: Notably, we observed an increase in the total immune cell population (CD45+) in both the caput and cauda of sham mice with most immune cell infiltrates observed at day 5, which returned to normal levels by day 14 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: An immune response was elicited in the absence of pathogens by surgery-associated trauma and ductal pressure due to the ligation of the vas deferens.
source: This indicated that an immune response was elicited in the absence of pathogens by surgery-associated trauma and ductal pressure due to the ligation of the vas deferens.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observation that sham mice showed immune cell infiltration.

claim: In the context of infection with UPEC, an increased infiltration of immune cells was observed in the cauda.
source: In the context of infection with UPEC, an increased infiltration of immune cells was observed in the cauda, whereas the caput showed a significant increase of immune cells compared to sham injected mice only at day 14 p.i. (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The caput showed a significant increase of immune cells compared to sham injected mice only at day 14 post infection.
source: In the context of infection with UPEC, an increased infiltration of immune cells was observed in the cauda, whereas the caput showed a significant increase of immune cells compared to sham injected mice only at day 14 p.i. (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Immune cell infiltration peaked at 10 days post infection, which correlated with disease score of the infected animals.
source: Immune cell infiltration peaked at 10 days p.i., which correlated with disease score of the infected animals (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: CX3CR1+ macrophages represented the most dominant immune cell population in the IS and caput.
source: CX3CR1+ macrophages represented the most dominant immune cell population in the IS and caput, whereas immune cell composition was more diverse in the corpus and cauda (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Immune cell composition was more diverse in the corpus and cauda compared to the IS and caput.
source: CX3CR1+ macrophages represented the most dominant immune cell population in the IS and caput, whereas immune cell composition was more diverse in the corpus and cauda (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry analysis shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Neutrophils were absent in samples from naive mice.
source: While neutrophils were absent in samples from naive mice, infiltrates of Gr-1+SSChi neutrophils (Figure 2E) and GR-1+SSClo monocytes (Figure 2F) were most pronounced in the corpus and cauda upon UPEC infection (Figure 2D–F. Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D-F and supplemental figures.

claim: Infiltrates of Gr-1+SSChi neutrophils and GR-1+SSClo monocytes were most pronounced in the corpus and cauda upon UPEC infection.
source: While neutrophils were absent in samples from naive mice, infiltrates of Gr-1+SSChi neutrophils (Figure 2E) and GR-1+SSClo monocytes (Figure 2F) were most pronounced in the corpus and cauda upon UPEC infection (Figure 2D–F. Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D-F and supplemental figures.

claim: Both corpus and cauda showed a significant increase in adaptive immune cell populations (B and T lymphocytes) after sham injection and UPEC infection.
source: Furthermore, both corpus and cauda showed a significant increase in adaptive immune cell populations (B and T lymphocytes), which were present after sham injection and UPEC infection (Figure 2G)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The increase in B and T cell populations correlated with the observed enrichment of gene sets associated with B and T cell activation at 10 days post infection.
source: Furthermore, both corpus and cauda showed a significant increase in adaptive immune cell populations (B and T lymphocytes), which were present after sham injection and UPEC infection (Figure 2G) and correlated with the observed enrichment of gene sets associated with B and T cell activation at 10 days p.i. (Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: This is a correlation between flow cytometry data (Figure 2G) and gene set enrichment analysis (Figure 1 supplement 3E).

claim: The ratio of CX3CR1+ macrophages significantly decreased in sham- and UPEC-infected mice compared to naive mice, particularly within the proximal regions (IS and caput).
source: Compared to naive mice the ratio of CX3CR1+ macrophages significantly decreased in sham- and UPEC-infected mice, particularly within the proximal regions (IS and caput, Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The decrease of CX3CR1+ macrophages in distal regions was accompanied by an increased ratio of CX3CR1- macrophages, indicating a shift in the macrophage pool.
source: In contrast to the proximal regions, the decrease of CX3CR1+ macrophages was accompanied by an increased ratio of CX3CR1- macrophages within the distal regions (corpus, cauda), indicating a shift in the macrophage pool (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2G and represents an interpretation of the data.

claim: A significantly increased ratio of CCR2+ cells within the total macrophages was observed in the corpus and cauda of UPEC-infected mice.
source: Notably, we observed a significantly increased ratio of CCR2+ cells within the total macrophages (CX3CR1+ and CX3CR1-) in the corpus and cauda of UPEC-infected mice (Figure 2H)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The increased ratio of CCR2+ cells within total macrophages indicates a potential contribution of monocytes to the macrophage pool within distal but not proximal regions upon UPEC infection.
source: Notably, we observed a significantly increased ratio of CCR2+ cells within the total macrophages (CX3CR1+ and CX3CR1-) in the corpus and cauda of UPEC-infected mice (Figure 2H), which indicates a potential contribution of monocytes to the macrophage pool within distal but not proximal regions upon UPEC infection.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The corpus and cauda developed a highly inflammatory immune environment in which subgroups of innate antigen-presenting myeloid (macrophages and cDC) and effector lymphoid cells co-existed.
source: Overall, the corpus and cauda developed a highly inflammatory immune environment in which subgroups of innate antigen-presenting myeloid (macrophages and cDC) and effector lymphoid cells co-existed.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the flow cytometry data presented in Figure 2.

claim: Sham-infected mice developed an inflammatory response with similar, yet milder changes in the immune cell composition compared to UPEC-infected mice.
source: In line with histological observations, also sham-infected mice developed an inflammatory response with similar, yet milder changes in the immune cell composition (Figure 2D–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2D-H.

claim: Numbers of Ly6G+ and Ly6C+ cells were progressively increasing within the interstitium of the cauda, but not the caput.
source: As seen by immunofluorescence analysis, numbers of Ly6G+ and Ly6C+ cells (including neutrophils and monocytes) were progressively increasing within the interstitium of the cauda, but not the caput, and also could be identified in the epididymal epithelium (Figure 2I)
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Ly6G+ and Ly6C+ cells could be identified in the epididymal epithelium at time points when epithelial integrity was disturbed.
source: As seen by immunofluorescence analysis, numbers of Ly6G+ and Ly6C+ cells (including neutrophils and monocytes) were progressively increasing within the interstitium of the cauda, but not the caput, and also could be identified in the epididymal epithelium (Figure 2I) at time points when epithelial integrity was disturbed.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The IS and caput were still mostly unreactive to LPS stimulation, while both corpus and cauda showed a significant upregulation of IL-1α, IL-1β, TNFα, MCP-1 (CCL2), IL-6, and IL-10.
source: While the IS and caput were still mostly unreactive, both corpus and cauda showed a significant upregulation of IL-1α, IL-1β, TNFα, MCP-1 (CCL2), IL-6, and IL-10 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo cytokine measurement data shown in Figure 2 supplement 3A.

claim: IS and caput showed a higher intracellular bacteria load compared to corpus and cauda after ex vivo co-culture of organ pieces with UPEC.
source: Intriguingly, IS and caput showed a higher intracellular bacteria load compared to corpus and cauda after ex vivo co-culture of organ pieces with UPEC, indicative for a higher and faster bacterial uptake and clearance potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by gentamicin assay data shown in Figure 2 supplement 3B.

claim: The higher intracellular bacteria load in IS and caput is indicative for a higher and faster bacterial uptake and clearance potential.
source: Intriguingly, IS and caput showed a higher intracellular bacteria load compared to corpus and cauda after ex vivo co-culture of organ pieces with UPEC, indicative for a higher and faster bacterial uptake and clearance potential (Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gentamicin assay data shown in Figure 2 supplement 3B.

claim: The fundamentally different immunological responses observed in vivo within different regions of the epididymis are an inherent feature of the region, and thus independent of the administration route of the inflammatory stimulus.
source: Overall, these data suggest that the fundamentally different immunological responses observed in vivo within different regions of the epididymis are an inherent feature of the region, and thus independent of the administration route of the inflammatory stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ex vivo experiments showing differential responses to simultaneous LPS stimulation.

claim: In total 12,966 cells were separately isolated from the four main epididymal regions (IS, caput, corpus, cauda) for scRNASeq analysis.
source: In total 12,966 cells were separately isolated from the four main epididymal regions (IS, caput, corpus, cauda).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure for scRNASeq.

claim: Unsupervised clustering and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) identified 13 different clusters.
source: Unsupervised clustering and uniform manifold approximation and projection (UMAP) identified 13 different clusters (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is supported by scRNASeq analysis shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The majority of identified immune cells comprised several myeloid cell populations including subsets of macrophages (clusters 1, 2, and 7), monocytes (clusters 8 and 10), and dendritic cells (clusters 2, 5, and 13).
source: Among the clusters, the majority of identified immune cells comprised several myeloid cell populations comprised several myeloid cell populations and included subsets of macrophages (clusters 1, 2, and 7), monocytes (clusters 8 and 10), and dendritic cells (clusters 2, 5, and 13).
evidence: This is based on the cluster identification from scRNASeq analysis.

claim: Macrophages were broadly identified by the co-expression of multiple key marker genes such as C1qa, Fcgr1 (encoding CD64), Adgre1 (encoding F4/80), and Cd68.
source: Macrophages were broadly identified by the co-expression of multiple key marker genes such as C1qa, Fcgr1 (encoding CD64), Adgre1 (encoding F4/80), and Cd68, with alternating levels of markers such as Cx3cr1, Ccr2, H2-Aa (encoding an MHC-II component).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data.

claim: Monocytes were broadly characterized by the expression of Ly6c2, Ccr2, and Ace.
source: Monocytes were broadly characterized by the expression of Ly6c2, Ccr2, and Ace.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data.

claim: Dendritic cells were segregated into three clusters that were identified as conventional DC 1 (Clec9a+Irf8+), conventional DC 2 (Cd209a+), and a small population of migratory DC (Ccr7+).
source: Dendritic cells (DC, Flt3+ high expression levels of MHC-II transcripts) were segregated into three clusters that were identified as conventional DC 1 (Clec9a+Irf8+), conventional DC 2 (Cd209a+), as well as a small population of migratory DC (Ccr7+, Figure 3B–E).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data shown in Figure 3B-E.

claim: All epididymal regions were populated by lymphocytes, including T cells (Cd3e+, clusters 4 and 9), NK cells (Nkg7+Eomes+, cluster 6), and B cells (Cd79a+, cluster 11).
source: Apart from myeloid cells, all epididymal regions were populated by lymphocytes, including T cells (Cd3e+, clusters 4 and 9), NK cells (Nkg7+Eomes+ , cluster 6), and B cells (Cd79a+, cluster 11, Figure 3D and E).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data shown in Figure 3D and E.

claim: T cells were further discriminated into αβ and γδ T cells based on their alternating expression of Trbc and Trdc, respectively.
source: T cells were further discriminated into αβ and γδ T cells based on their alternating expression of Trbc and Trdc, respectively.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data.

claim: The vast majority of resident immune cells in the epididymis were found in the IS (approximately 10-15% CD45+ cells among the single live cells vs. 1-5% CD45+ cells in single live cells in caput to cauda).
source: The vast majority of resident immune cells in the epididymis were found in the IS (approximately 10–15% CD45+ cells among the single live cells vs. 1–5% CD45+ cells in single live cells in caput to cauda; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: IS and caput were predominantly populated by macrophage subsets (approximately 78% and 66% in CD45+ cells, respectively).
source: In this regard, IS and caput were predominantly populated by macrophage subsets (approximately 78% and 66% in CD45+ cells, respectively; Figure 4B)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In IS and caput, other leukocytes accounted for <5% for each population.
source: In this regard, IS and caput were predominantly populated by macrophage subsets (approximately 78% and 66% in CD45+ cells, respectively; Figure 4B) with other leukocytes accounting for <5% for each population (Figure 4B–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B-H.

claim: The corpus and cauda contained a more heterogeneous immune cell network, including several myeloid cell populations.
source: In contrast, the corpus and cauda contained a more heterogeneous immune cell network, including several myeloid cell populations.
evidence: This is a summary of the flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data.

claim: In corpus and cauda, macrophages constituted 25-35% of CD45+ cells.
source: In addition to macrophages (25–35%, Figure 4B), monocytes (7–10%, Figure 4C) and dendritic cells (cDC1 7–10% and cDC2: 12–20%, Figure 4D and E) were predominantly found in close conjunction with the epididymal duct, as detected by immunofluorescence analysis.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In corpus and cauda, monocytes constituted 7-10% of CD45+ cells.
source: In addition to macrophages (25–35%, Figure 4B), monocytes (7–10%, Figure 4C) and dendritic cells (cDC1 7–10% and cDC2: 12–20%, Figure 4D and E) were predominantly found in close conjunction with the epididymal duct, as detected by immunofluorescence analysis.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In corpus and cauda, cDC1 constituted 7-10% and cDC2 constituted 12-20% of CD45+ cells.
source: In addition to macrophages (25–35%, Figure 4B), monocytes (7–10%, Figure 4C) and dendritic cells (cDC1 7–10% and cDC2: 12–20%, Figure 4D and E) were predominantly found in close conjunction with the epididymal duct, as detected by immunofluorescence analysis.
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4D and E.

claim: Monocytes and dendritic cells were predominantly found in close conjunction with the epididymal duct in corpus and cauda.
source: In addition to macrophages (25–35%, Figure 4B), monocytes (7–10%, Figure 4C) and dendritic cells (cDC1 7–10% and cDC2: 12–20%, Figure 4D and E) were predominantly found in close conjunction with the epididymal duct, as detected by immunofluorescence analysis.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 4C-E.

claim: No plasmacytoid dendritic cells were found within the murine epididymis.
source: In accordance with the previous studies (Voisin et al., 2018), no plasmacytoid dendritic cells were found within the murine epididymis.
evidence: This is supported by the current study's findings and corroborated by citation to Voisin et al., 2018.

claim: Lymphocyte subsets (NK cells [10%], B cells [2-5%], T cells [10-20%]) were located in both the interstitial and intraepithelial compartment.
source: Lymphocyte subsets (NK cells [10%, Figure 4F], B cells [2–5%, Figure 4G], T cells [10–20%, Figure 4H]) were located in both the interstitial and intraepithelial compartment (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Among the T cells, αβ and γδ T cells were distinguished, with only the latter found within the epithelium.
source: Among the T cells, we further distinguished αβ and γδ T cells, with only the latter found within the epithelium (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: The proximal and distal regions showed striking differences in their immunological landscapes.
source: The difference in leukocyte populations, their ratio, and tissue localization throughout the epididymis points to the existence of inherently different immunological environments in the proximal (IS, caput) and distal regions (corpus, cauda), which form the basis of the differential immune responsiveness observed in models of epididymitis.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the flow cytometry and immunofluorescence data.

claim: Resident immune cells are strategically positioned along the epididymal duct, potentially providing different immunological environments required for addressing the contrasting immunological challenges.
source: These findings indicate that resident immune cells are strategically positioned along the epididymal duct, potentially providing different immunological environments required for addressing the contrasting immunological challenges and thus, preserving tissue integrity and organ function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall findings of the study.

claim: Adgre1+C1qa+ cells, broadly considered as macrophages, constitute the majority of CD45+ cells in the epididymis.
source: Adgre1+C1qa + cells, broadly considered as macrophages (Dick et al., 2022), constitute the majority of CD45+ cells in the epididymis.
evidence: This is based on scRNASeq data and supported by citation to Dick et al., 2022.

claim: Macrophage populations (clusters 1, 2, and 7) were distinguished from monocyte populations (clusters 8 and 10) based on their expression of C1qa, Ccr2, Ly6c2, Napsa, and Plac8.
source: In subsequent closer analyses with the aim to decipher the possible heterogeneity of this population, we first distinguished macrophage populations (clusters 1, 2, and 7) from monocyte populations (clusters 8 and 10) based on their expression of C1qa, Ccr2, Ly6c2, Napsa, and Plac8 (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Both monocyte clusters expressed lower levels of C1qa compared to macrophage clusters.
source: In subsequent closer analyses with the aim to decipher the possible heterogeneity of this population, we first distinguished macrophage populations (clusters 1, 2, and 7) from monocyte populations (clusters 8 and 10) based on their expression of C1qa, Ccr2, Ly6c2, Napsa, and Plac8 (Figure 5A), with both monocyte clusters expressing lower levels of C1qa.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Cluster 10 showed higher expression of transcripts encoding classical monocyte markers (Ly6c2, Napsa, Plac8) compared to cluster 8.
source: However, cluster 10 showed higher expression of transcripts encoding classical monocyte markers (Ly6c2, Napsa, Plac8) compared to cluster 8.
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data.

claim: Cluster 10 resembles a classical monocyte population, whereas cluster 8 represents a monocyte population undergoing differentiation into a macrophage phenotype.
source: This indicates that cluster 10 resembles a classical monocyte population, whereas cluster 8 represents a monocyte population undergoing differentiation into a macrophage phenotype.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the gene expression patterns observed in scRNASeq data.

claim: Cluster 8 showed intermediate expression of C1qa, Adgre1, and Fcgr1 between classical monocytes (cluster 10) and macrophage populations (clusters 1, 2, and 7).
source: This assumption was also supported by intermediate expression of C1qa, Adgre1, and Fcgr1 between classical monocytes (cluster 10) and macrophage populations (clusters 1, 2, and 7, Figure 3D, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis from scRNASeq data shown in Figure 3D and 5A.

claim: By unsupervised clustering of macrophage subpopulations (clusters 1, 2, and 7), nine subgroups were identified.
source: By unsupervised clustering, nine subgroups (Figure 5B) were identified, each with a distinct gene expression profile (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on re-clustering analysis of scRNASeq data shown in Figure 5B and C.

claim: All identified macrophage subgroups were highly enriched with C1qa and Adgre1 transcripts confirming their macrophage identity.

evidence: This is supported by the flow cytometry and histological data presented in the study.

claim: Both neutrophils and monocyte-derived macrophages are important first defenders of the innate immune response during acute infection due to their high phagocytic activity.
source: Both neutrophils and monocyte-derived macrophages are important first defenders of the innate immune response during acute infection due to their high phagocytic activity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established scientific knowledge about innate immunity.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Segel et al., 2011 and Kruger et al., 2015.

claim: Ccr2-/- mice show a significantly reduced influx of neutrophils and inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages concomitant with less severe tissue damage in the cauda during UPEC infection compared to wild type mice.

Ccr2-/- mice show a significantly reduced influx of neutrophils and inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages concomitant with less severe tissue damage in the cauda during UPEC infection compared to wild type mice (Wang et al., 2021)
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2021.

source: Ccr2-/- mice show a significantly reduced influx of neutrophils and inflammatory monocyte-derived macrophages concomitant with less severe tissue damage in the cauda during UPEC infection compared to wild type mice (Wang et al., 2021) pointing to a role as double-edged swords in acute epididymitis by participating in both defense and inflammation-associated tissue damage.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the findings from Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Bacterial virulence factors may contribute to some extent to tissue damage in the cauda following the observation that UPEC persist in this region much longer and at higher numbers than in the other parts of the organ.

evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism of persisting immunopathology.

claim: The data unravel the transcriptional identity and tissue location of extravascular immune cells and further support the existence of distinct immunological environments along the epididymal duct.

evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study's findings.

claim: The transcriptional profile of intraepithelial CX3CR1+ cells combined with the known high phagocytic potential indicates a central function in tissue homeostasis and immune surveillance.
source: The transcriptional profile of intraepithelial CX3CR1+ cells combined with the known high phagocytic potential toward apoptotic epithelial cells (i.e. within the IS, Smith et al., 2014) and pathogens (Battistone et al., 2020) indicates a central function in tissue homeostasis and immune surveillance in order to efficiently maintain epithelial integrity that in turn is mandatory for maintaining the luminal microenvironment required for proper sperm maturation.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the transcriptional profile data and supported by citations to Smith et al., 2014 and Battistone et al., 2020.

claim: The high density of sensing CX3CR1hi macrophages in combination with the narrow lumen of the IS indicates a potential function of this region as 'immunological bottleneck'.
source: Of note, the high density of sensing CX3CR1hi macrophages in combination with the narrow lumen of the IS indicates a potential function of this region as 'immunological bottleneck' in which the luminal content is constantly monitored in order to induce tolerance toward immunogenic sperm antigens and to eliminate pathogens from further ascend to the testis.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the macrophage distribution and anatomical features of the IS.

claim: The co-existence of antigen-presenting myeloid cell populations with lymphocyte subtypes within the distal regions of the epididymis implies an environment of immune responsiveness.
source: The co-existence of antigen-presenting myeloid cell populations (macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells) with lymphocyte subtypes (NK cells, αβ T cells, γδ T cells, B cells) within the distal regions of the epididymis implies an environment of immune responsiveness.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immune cell composition data.

claim: The existence of intraepithelial and interstitial lymphocyte subpopulations with innate-like characteristics (i.e. NK cells, γδ T cells), predominantly within the distal regions, implies a contribution of these cells to the onset of immune responses against pathogens.

evidence: This is an interpretation of the lymphocyte distribution data.

claim: NK cells and γδ T cells generally function as key responders to barrier stress signals in mucosal tissues and accelerate pro-inflammatory processes by secreting effector cytokines, particularly IL-17 and IFNγ.
source: Both populations generally function as key responders to barrier stress signals in mucosal tissues and accelerate pro-inflammatory processes by secreting effector cytokines, particularly IL-17- and IFNγ (Shi et al., 2011; Papotto et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shi et al., 2011 and Papotto et al., 2017.

claim: The function of innate lymphoid cells highly depends on their activation status and functional polarization within the periphery.
source: Since the function of innate lymphoid cells highly depends on their activation status and functional polarization within the periphery (Bonneville et al., 2010; Klose and Artis, 2020), local environmental factors may determine regulatory vs. cytotoxic functions of NK and γδ T cells in different epididymal regions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bonneville et al., 2010 and Klose and Artis, 2020.

claim: Local environmental factors may determine regulatory vs. cytotoxic functions of NK and γδ T cells in different epididymal regions.
source: Since the function of innate lymphoid cells highly depends on their activation status and functional polarization within the periphery (Bonneville et al., 2010; Klose and Artis, 2020), local environmental factors may determine regulatory vs. cytotoxic functions of NK and γδ T cells in different epididymal regions.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the known biology of innate lymphoid cells.

claim: The scRNASeq approach supplies 'only' a snapshot of extravascular immune cells within the epididymis at a defined time (in the adult).
source: As a limitation, our scRNASeq approach supplies 'only' a snapshot of extravascular immune cells within the epididymis at a defined time (in the adult) neglecting times of residency for, for example, myeloid and lymphoid immune cell populations that possess migratory capabilities and patrol between non-lymphoid tissues and draining lymph nodes, a process required for immune surveillance and induction of immune responses or tolerance (Hampton and Chtanova, 2019).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation of the study methodology.

claim: The data provide the first atlas of extravascular CD45+ cells within the murine epididymis under normal conditions.
source: Together, our data provide the first atlas of extravascular CD45+ cells within the murine epididymis under normal conditions.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the study's contribution.

claim: Strategic positioning of identified immune cell populations strongly indicates the existence of distinct immunological landscapes at the opposing ends of the epididymal duct.
source: Strategic positioning of identified immune cell populations strongly indicates the existence of distinct immunological landscapes at the opposing ends of the epididymal duct that, in turn, is considered as a main driver for the observed differences in the intensity of immune responsiveness upon bacterial infection.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immune cell distribution data.
